title: Polishing and paint correction: the difference
audience: Car detailers who inspect, measure and correct paint defects, and who must recognise when a panel needs referral instead of correction.
learningOutcomes: Explain what polishing removes, and why correction removes more material than a finishing polish.
Identify the paint system with a test, and record the result before choosing products.
Choose the least aggressive product and pad combination that works, and step up only after a recorded test.
Inspect each panel under a directional light and measure its paint thickness with a calibrated gauge, recording the readings before any correction.
Refer or decline a panel when a referral trigger applies, such as thin or uneven clear coat, a prior repair, a deep defect or clear-coat failure, and record that decision.
Run the compounding, polishing and finishing sequence panel by panel, with heat and residue checks, and state the PPE and SDS controls that apply before work starts.

instruction.heading: What correction is, and what it is not
instruction.body: Polishing levels the clear coat. Correction is the wider term: it covers any abrasive step that removes a measured amount of paint to reduce a defect, and it takes away more material than a finishing polish does. The difference matters because clear coat is a finite layer. Each cut removes some of it, and that loss cannot be reversed. Waxes, sealants and glazes can hide some defects for a while, but they leave the surface itself unchanged. A correction job is therefore a decision about how much material to remove, from which panel, for which defect, and within limits agreed in advance. That is why this lesson puts inspection, measurement and referral ahead of any machine work. Basis: the principle that polishing levels the surface and removes thin material is drawn from the Auto-Detailing guide and the show-car sample, reworded. The decision process and the limits are working practice.

instruction.heading: Paint defects and how they differ
instruction.body: Each defect looks different, has a different cause and has a different limit. Swirls are fine, curved marks that show mainly in direct light. The Auto-Detailing guide describes them as very thin, shallow scratches that scatter light instead of letting it pass through the clear coat, which dulls the finish. Light scratches run in straighter lines or in random directions, and they cut deeper than swirls, so they catch a fingernail more readily. Oxidation is a dull, chalky or hazy change in the surface. The show-car sample notes that single-stage paint oxidises more readily than clear-coated paint, so it is most often met on older vehicles. Water spotting is a mineral deposit left when water dries. If it sits too long it can etch the surface, and the Auto-Detailing guide sorts water spots into three types by how deep they have gone. Etching is damage to the clear coat from a deposit or contaminant that has sat on the paint, and it can remain after the deposit has gone. Basis: the list of imperfections and the water-spot types are from the Auto-Detailing guide. The single-stage oxidation point is from the show-car sample. The fingernail check is working practice: it is a rough guide to depth, not a measurement.

instruction.heading: Inspection under lighting
instruction.body: Inspect before any product or machine touches the paint. Wash and decontaminate first, as “Clay bar and decontamination” describes, because contamination hides defects and can scratch under a pad. Use a directional light held at a low angle, and check each panel from several angles, since a defect can vanish from one direction and show clearly from another. Walk the vehicle in a fixed order and mark each defect on a diagram or photograph it with a reference point, so the record can be matched to the panel later. Compare each panel with its neighbours. A panel that looks different from the rest is often the first sign of a prior repair. Repeat the inspection under the same type of light after each stage of correction, so that results can be compared. Basis: working practice. The directional-light method is also used in the guides, reworded.

instruction.heading: Measuring paint thickness
instruction.body: A paint thickness gauge reads total film build, which is the combined thickness of primer, colour and clear coat if present. It does not read the clear coat alone, so a single reading cannot tell you how much clear is left to cut. Calibrate the gauge before use on a reference shim of known thickness, following the instrument's own instructions. The show-car sample describes recalibrating its gauge on a shim before trusting any reading. Gauges also differ in accuracy. The sample compares a more accurate class of gauge with a common less accurate one, and notes that the difference matters most on coatings that are already thin. Take several readings on each panel, spread across the panel and kept away from edges, trim, badges and stickers. Record each reading, the average and any outlier, along with the gauge model, the calibration method and the date. Units matter: one mil is 25.4 micrometres, so the sample's figure of about 2 mil is about 50.8 micrometres. The sample also says the figure varies by manufacturer, so compare a vehicle with its own panels, not with a figure from a table. Example figures only, not standards: a door reading 110 micrometres when the other panels read about 90 micrometres is a difference to record and refer, not a number to correct down to. Basis: the mil-to-micrometre conversion is arithmetic. The calibration, accuracy and total-film points are from the show-car sample, reworded. The reading procedure and recording are working practice.

instruction.heading: Identifying the paint system and why test spots come first
instruction.body: Most cars built since the 1980s have a basecoat with a clear coat over it. Single-stage paint has its colour through one layer and no separate clear. The show-car sample describes single-stage paint as softer and more prone to oxidising, which changes how it polishes. A pad test can help tell them apart. Polish a small area with a light-coloured pad, then check the pad. If colour transfers onto it, the pigment runs through the layer, which suggests single-stage paint. A clean pad suggests a clear coat. Tinted clear coats can mislead, so test each panel instead of assuming the whole vehicle matches. A test spot is a small, representative area, usually low-visibility, where you try the process before any wider work. The show-car sample calls this dialling in. Start with the least aggressive combination. If it does not work quickly enough, step up one variable at a time, either the product or the pad, and test again. A test that fails is information, so it tells you to stop and reassess rather than push harder. Record the area, the product, the pad, the machine setting range from the label or tool manual, the passes and the result. Photograph the result under the same light used for inspection. Basis: the test-spot and dialling-in concept is from the show-car sample, reworded. The pad-test interpretation and the tinted-clear caution are working practice. Speeds, passes and dwell times come from the product label and the tool manual, not from this lesson.

instruction.heading: When to refer rather than correct
instruction.body: Some panels should not be corrected in-house. Refer, or decline and record, when any of these triggers applies, and tell the owner in writing. Thin clear coat, or clear coat that reads thin in places, leaves little margin, so a cut can go through to colour. A reading well above the rest of the vehicle suggests filler, a respray or another prior repair, and that repair is outside detailing. A defect that catches a fingernail, or a scratch that reaches the colour, needs a qualified repairer to assess options. Clear-coat failure, where the clear peels, lifts or cracks, cannot be levelled, and abrasive work only exposes more damage. The show-car sample describes this failure as a breakdown the layer cannot recover from, with repainting as the remedy. Edges, panel seams, plastic trim and paint around sensors or badges are also high-risk areas. Basis: the clear-coat failure point is from the show-car sample. The triggers themselves, and the thresholds the business sets for them, are working practice. No number in this lesson is a universal limit.

instruction.heading: Sequence: compounding, polishing and finishing
instruction.body: Correction runs from the most aggressive step to the least, and each step leaves the surface ready for the next. Compounding is the cutting step. It removes the deepest defects and usually leaves marring that a finer step must refine. Polishing refines the surface and removes lighter marring. Finishing removes micro-marring, haze and very light swirls, and brings out gloss. The Auto-Detailing guide notes that finishing polishes generally cannot remove imperfections deeper than a very light swirl. Do not skip steps to save time, and do not use a compound where a finishing polish already gives the agreed result. Between steps, wipe the surface clean and inspect it, so that you can see what the last step achieved. Move to the next step only after a recorded test, as the procedure below sets out. Basis: the three-level description is from the Auto-Detailing guide, reworded. The step order as a working rule, and the decision to move between steps, are working practice. The number of steps is a business decision, recorded in the approved SOP.

instruction.heading: Pads and products in general terms
instruction.body: Pads and products are chosen as a pair, and the pair should match the defect. A firmer pad used with a cutting product removes more material. A softer, finer pad used with a finishing product refines the surface. Foam pads differ in density, thickness and diameter, and each changes how much cut and how much heat the pad produces. Some pads use grooves, a centre hole or a beveled edge to help reduce heat, and the Car-Detailing-Guide describes such designs. Wool and microfibre pads are used for cutting and for some polishing steps, and they behave differently from foam. Clean or replace pads as the job requires, because a loaded pad cuts unevenly and can scratch. Each product label states the surfaces it is for, how to apply it and how to remove it. Follow the label, and do not mix products unless the label allows it. The Spanish-language manual reports that some protectants should be applied by hand only, which the label governs. Basis: the aggressiveness principle and the heat-reducing pad designs are from the Auto-Detailing guide and the Car-Detailing-Guide, reworded. Product choice is decided by the test spot, not by a table in this lesson. Brand names and product-specific settings are not used here.

instruction.heading: Machine choice, speed and heat
instruction.body: Dual-action and random orbital machines oscillate, which makes them safer for learners and less likely to burn paint than a rotary machine. A rotary machine spins the pad on one axis, removes material faster and needs more practice. The Auto-Detailing guide treats rotary buffers as a tool for experienced detailers only. The detailing handbook excerpt warns that high-speed buffing can burn through clear coat when a pad is held in one place. Speed should come from the machine's manual and the product label, not from memory or from this lesson. A common working rule is to start with a lower speed to spread product and then increase only as the test requires. Reduce speed and pad firmness as the process moves toward finishing. The Spanish-language manual makes the same point: firmer pads at higher speed early in the process, and softer pads at lower speed later. Control heat by keeping the machine moving, using light pressure, avoiding edges and high spots, and stopping to check the surface by hand. If the panel feels hot, or the product is drying out, stop, let the panel cool and re-wet the area as the product label directs. Stop at once for smoke, a burning smell or a sudden change in gloss that you cannot account for. Basis: the rotary-versus-orbital comparison and the handbook warning are from the Auto-Detailing guide and the detailing handbook excerpt, reworded. The speed-sequence rule is from the Spanish-language manual, reworded. The touch check and stop rules are working practice.

instruction.heading: Working panel by panel, residue and final inspection
instruction.body: Work in small sections, one panel at a time, so that you can control coverage and inspect each area before moving on. Before you start, tape off trim, badges, panel gaps and edges with full strips of tape, and cover glass and fragile parts. Apply product in controlled amounts, and spread it before the machine runs. Work each section to the test result, then move on. Polish residue is the main reason a result looks worse than it is. When the polish breaks down it can look like a clear or milky haze, and that haze can hide both the defect and the result. When you see it, stop the machine, wipe the area with a clean microfibre and inspect under the directional light. Refold towels to a clean face often, and keep each product's towels separate. Basis: the section-by-section approach is from the Auto-Detailing guide, reworded. The breakdown-haze observation is from the Auto-Detailing guide. The tape, towel and final-inspection steps are working practice. Record a final inspection of each panel under the same light, compared with the reference panel, before protection is applied.

instruction.heading: Protection after correction, and removing residue
instruction.body: Once the surface is level and clean, protection locks in the result. Remove residue first with a clean microfibre. If the product label or the surface calls for a wipe-down before protection, use a product whose SDS and label cover that use, and apply the controls the SDS lists. Choose a protectant listed for the surface, such as a sealant or a wax, and apply it as the label directs. Some protectants are hand-applied only, and the label decides the method. Wipe off the excess so nothing pools on trim or edges. Do not promise durability. Tell the owner that protection needs regular maintenance and that deep defects remain. Coatings and ceramic products are not taught in this lesson. Any claim about how long a coating lasts or what it does needs evidence the business can support, and the ACCC point below applies to it. Basis: the protection steps are working practice, with the hand-applied note taken from the Spanish-language manual, reworded.

instruction.heading: Safety: PPE, vibration, electrical equipment and machines
instruction.body: Start with the controls that remove or reduce the hazard, and treat PPE as the last line. The WorkSafe Victoria hierarchy of control places personal protective equipment at the bottom. It describes PPE as a last resort or a temporary measure while a better control is put in place, so it does not replace guarding, layout or safe procedures. Eye protection: wear it for all polishing and cleaning tasks, because splatter and pad debris can reach the eye. Gloves and any other PPE: follow the SDS of each product. Respiratory protection: a polisher used on a clear-coated panel is not expected to create airborne dust. If an SDS names a respiratory hazard, or a task produces dust or mist, such as sanding, wet abrasive work or heavy product fallout, use respiratory protection at the level the SDS and a risk assessment require. Sanding and wet abrasive work are not taught in this lesson. Hand-arm vibration: Safe Work Australia lists exposure to vibration among the risk factors for musculoskeletal disorders, and it publishes a guide to managing hand-arm vibration. In practice, lighter machines, shorter sessions and breaks reduce exposure, and Safe Work Australia's guidance on manual tasks recommends rotating workers between repetitive tasks. Electrical safety: check cords and plugs before use, keep cords clear of the work area and pads, and keep electrical equipment away from water. Machine guarding: check the backing plate, the pad fitting and any guard or shroud the manufacturer fitted, and never run a machine with a part missing. Product SDS: read the SDS for each product before use and note its flammable, irritant and respiratory warnings. Safe Work Australia states that almost every hazardous chemical needs an SDS, and that copies must be kept in the workplace.

instruction.heading: Claims, documentation and the record
instruction.body: A claim about the result must match what you showed. The ACCC states that a business's intention does not matter, and that leaving out important information can make a claim misleading. A statement that all swirls have been removed, when the test covered one door, is a problem even if you did not mean to mislead. Describe the likely result and its limits, and record them. Keep a record for each job: the paint-system note, the thickness readings with gauge model and calibration, the test spot record, each referral or decline with photographs, the products and pads with their label or SDS references, the passes, the final inspection, the protection applied and the owner's acknowledgement. Keep the record with the job file, so that the next detailer can see what was done and why. Basis: the ACCC principles are sourced from the ACCC page. The documentation list is working practice.

procedure: Wash and decontaminate the vehicle as “Clay bar and decontamination” sets out, and check the surface is clean before inspection.
Inspect each panel under a directional light from several angles, and record each defect by type and location.
Calibrate the paint thickness gauge on its reference shim, then take several readings on each panel away from edges and trim, and record them.
Identify the paint system on each panel with the pad test on a low-visibility area, and record the result.
Refer or decline any panel that meets a referral trigger, and record the decision and the owner's notification.
Read the SDS and label for each product, and put on the PPE the SDS names. Check the machine, pad fitting and cords before use.
Set up a test spot with the least aggressive combination on a representative, low-visibility area.
Run the test with light pressure, keep the machine moving, check the surface by hand at intervals, and stop when the polish breaks down or the panel feels hot.
Wipe the test area clean and assess it under the directional light. Record the area, product, pad, machine setting range from the label or tool manual, passes and result.
If the test does not work, step up one variable only, repeat the test, and stop if the next step is not agreed.
Work the agreed area section by section and panel by panel, with tape on trim and edges, and stop at any sign of haze, heat or a change in gloss.
Finish with the finishing step, wipe the residue clean, and re-inspect each panel under the same light against the reference panel.
Protect the surface with a product listed for it, applied as its label directs, and record the products, the final inspection and the owner's acknowledgement.

workedExamples.situation: A nine-year-old black car has a dull, hazy look and swirl marks on the doors. The owner wants the marks gone.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What do you inspect and measure first, and what do you tell the owner?
workedExamples.reasoning: Wash and decontaminate, then inspect each panel under a directional light. Calibrate the thickness gauge and take several readings on each door and on the roof, and record them. Identify the paint system with the pad test. If the readings are even and not thin, set up a test spot on a low-visibility area of a door with the least aggressive finishing polish and a matched pad. If the test removes the haze and the light swirls without damage, repeat the process across the car with the owner's agreement. Tell the owner that the result depends on the paint, that deep marks may remain, and that the likely result and its limits are recorded. If the test does not work, step up one variable only, record it, and stop if the next step is not agreed. (Example reading figures are for teaching only.)

workedExamples.situation: A silver car's clear coat is peeling in a patch on the roof. A colleague offers a more aggressive compound to smooth it out.
workedExamples.reasoning: Do not start the compound. Record the peeling as a possible clear-coat failure, note its location and photograph it under a directional light. Take thickness readings around the patch to inform the referral. Explain that abrasive work will expose more damage and cannot restore the clear coat. Refer the owner to a qualified repairer for an assessment of repair options, because repainting is outside detailing. Decline the aggressive correction and record the decline with the owner's acknowledgement.

workedExamples.situation: A white car's front bonnet reads well above the other panels with the gauge, and the owner asks for the whole car to be corrected to a mirror finish.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which panel do you treat first, and what do you agree with the owner?
workedExamples.reasoning: Record the high readings and check the panel's edges and seams for signs of a respray. Treat the bonnet as a possible prior repair and refer it, rather than correct it in-house. On the rest of the car, inspect and test as usual, starting with a test spot on a low-visibility area. Tell the owner that a mirror finish cannot be promised, that the bonnet is excluded and why, and that the result on the other panels will be recorded. Do not agree to an outcome you cannot show in a test.

equipmentAndPpe: Dual-action or random orbital polisher, with a backing plate matched to the pad size.
Rotary machine only under experienced supervision and only after training.
Pads by aggressiveness, cleaned or replaced regularly, and kept separate by product.
Polishes and compounds at each level, used as their labels direct.
Calibrated paint thickness gauge with its reference shim, and a record sheet for readings.
Directional light, clean microfibre towels and masking tape for trim and edges.
PPE: eye protection and gloves as each SDS requires. Respiratory protection only where an SDS or risk assessment names it. Remove rings, watches and loose buttons before work.

commonErrors.prevention: Test on a representative, low-visibility area and record the result.

commonErrors.error: Starting with the most aggressive product.
commonErrors.prevention: Start with the least aggressive combination and step up one variable at a time.

commonErrors.error: Reading a thickness gauge without calibrating it, or reading on edges, trim or stickers.
commonErrors.prevention: Calibrate on the reference shim before use. Take several readings per panel, away from edges, trim and stickers, and record each one.

commonErrors.error: Treating a high or uneven reading as a normal panel.
commonErrors.prevention: Record it, check the neighbouring panels, and refer it before any correction.

commonErrors.error: Using a rotary machine without training.
commonErrors.prevention: Use a dual-action or random orbital machine until trained. Rotary work needs supervision.

commonErrors.error: Working on edges, panel seams and high spots.
commonErrors.prevention: Tape off edges and seams, keep the machine off high spots, and reduce pressure near them.

commonErrors.error: Continuing after the polish has broken down, or after the panel has become hot.
commonErrors.prevention: Stop, let the panel cool if needed, wipe, and inspect under a directional light.

commonErrors.error: Promising full removal of marks, or a finish the test did not show.
commonErrors.prevention: Describe the likely result and its limits, and record them.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Claims about correction results must be accurate and supportable. The ACCC states that intent does not matter, and that leaving out important information can mislead (ACCC: false or misleading claims).

Safe Work Australia states that almost every hazardous chemical needs a safety data sheet, and that copies must be kept in the workplace. Read the SDS for each product before use, and apply the PPE and handling controls it lists.
The WorkSafe Victoria hierarchy of control places PPE last, as a temporary or supporting measure. Use layout, equipment choice and safe procedures first.
Exposure to vibration is listed by Safe Work Australia as a risk factor for musculoskeletal disorders. Use lighter machines, shorter sessions and rotation between tasks as working controls.
Check cords and plugs on machines before use, keep cords off wet ground and clear of pads, and keep electrical equipment away from water.

Panel repair, filler work, respraying and sanding-based defect removal are outside this lesson and are for a qualified repairer. This lesson does not grant any licence or authority to carry out those repairs.

qualityStandard: The paint system is identified and recorded for each panel.
Calibrated thickness readings are recorded for each panel, and any panel that meets a referral trigger is referred or declined in writing.
A test spot with the least aggressive combination comes before any wider work, and its result is recorded.
No step-up is applied without a recorded test result and the owner's agreement.
No panel is worked on past the point where the polish has broken down, and residue is removed before the final inspection.
documentationEvidence: Paint system note and photographs under a directional light.
Thickness record: gauge model, calibration method and date, each reading and the average, with the panel named.
Test spot record: area, product, pad, machine setting range from the label or tool manual, passes and result.
Referral, decline or owner-notification record, with photographs and the owner's acknowledgement.
Final inspection record for each panel, and the protection product used, with its label or SDS reference.
summary: Correction removes a finite layer of clear coat, so inspect and measure before any product or machine touches the paint.
Identify the paint system and test the least aggressive combination first, then step up one variable at a time.
Refer or decline a panel that shows thin or uneven clear coat, a prior repair, a deep defect or clear-coat failure, and record the decision.
Control heat, residue and machine work panel by panel, and wear the PPE and follow the SDS each product names.
Describe the likely result and its limits, and record everything so the claim matches the work.

knowledgeChecks.question: What does a finishing polish typically achieve?
options: Removes deep scratches down to the primer layer
Replaces the clear coat on the whole panel
Seals the paint for twelve months at a time
Removes micro-marring, haze and very light swirls

knowledgeChecks.question: Colour transfers onto a light-coloured pad during a test. What does this suggest?
options: A clear-coat finish with no defects showing under the light at all
A single-stage paint, where the colour runs through the whole layer
A wax on the surface, which would not leave colour on the pad at all
Tinted glass, which is common on the side windows of most cars

knowledgeChecks.question: A test spot shows no improvement with the least aggressive product. What is the correct next step?
options: Use the most aggressive compound across the car to finish the whole job faster
Skip the test and polish the car anyway, since the test is not needed for most cars
Apply a wax to hide the marks, so the customer does not notice them at handover
Step up one variable, record the result, and stop if the next step is not agreed

knowledgeChecks.question: A paint thickness gauge reads well above the other panels on one door. What is the most cautious response?
options: Polish the door harder until it matches the other panels, which should even out the reading quickly
Record the reading as a possible prior repair, check the neighbouring panels, and refer before any correction
Ignore the reading, because thickness does not affect the correction decision made on the day at the car
Remove the surface with the most aggressive compound to bring the reading down to match the others
